I will start by apologizing, because I was distracted so I accidentally thought it was "why is systemd bad" instead of "why is systemd a back door."

To elaborate - I am pretty sure there is no known, intentional backdoor into systemd, at least in terms of the "instant access to bypass security measures" type, so the systemd guys won't (necessarily and intentionally) be able to use all the systemd-running systems to mount a DDoS attack on some poor schmuck. Not many projects could manage to survive such a scandal, and given it's OSS it is one of the few things that would result in a fork that would almost certainly leave the original to die a slow and lingering death (probably making the XFree86 tussle look like a minor spat).

It might however be considered something of a trojan. Not in the technical sense, but more along the lines of the political sense, in terms of who leverages power over what parts of the Linux ecosystem. It concentrates a considerable amount of effort and options into one solid "does all" package and can easily be used to starve off a lot of potential alternatives, consolidating the influence on just a handful of developers. It also means that most systemd systems will share a lot of vulnerabilities in a core service. There are a variety of potential implications due to this, most of them not particularly good. It also means that "one size fits all" results in everyone having to cram into that one size, so instead of "systemd fits all cases" you get "all cases are crammed in to fit systemd," which does not have a great outcome.

That said, some of this could also be said to be similar with init.d, but there's a lot more custom code involved in setting up init.d since it relies so heavily on scripts, making it more difficult, at least in theory, to replicate the exact same vulnerability everywhere.
